cues.text: Harrowmere lies at the head of a long valley, where three rivers meet and slow into a lake.
In winter the lake is still and grey.
Mist sits on the water until late morning,
and the far shore can be lost from sight for days at a time.
The village of Caerwen stands on the eastern shore.
It has one street, one inn and a small stone church,
and a little over four hundred people live there all year round.
Most of them make their living from the lake, as their families always have.
Before the road was built, the only way in or out was by water.
Tamsin Vey runs the ferry now, as her father did before her.
She makes the crossing to the western shore six times a day in summer,
and twice a day in winter, when the wind allows.
The crossing takes about twenty minutes.
On a calm morning it is the quietest journey in the valley.
Out in the middle of the lake lies Sgeirra, a low island of rock and pine.
Nobody has lived there for more than a century,
but the ruins of a small farm can still be seen from the ferry.
In spring the snow on the high ground begins to melt.
The rivers rise quickly.
Within a week the lake climbs by almost two metres,
and the meadows along the northern edge vanish under a sheet of shallow water.
For the birds, this is the best time of the year.
Herons stand in the flooded grass.
Geese arrive from the south in long, untidy lines.
And on still evenings, the calls of the curlew carry across the whole valley.
By May the water has gone down again.
The fields are cut for hay in the first dry weeks of June.
Every farm in the valley helps with the harvest, moving from one field to the next until all of it is in.
On the steeper slopes the work is still done by hand.
At the northern end of the lake stands an old water mill.
It ground corn for Caerwen's bakers for nearly three hundred years,
and it still turns on open days, though only for visitors now.
Summer brings walkers.
Some come for a single afternoon, others for weeks.
The path around the lake is twenty-two kilometres long.
Most people walk it in two days, stopping for the night at the inn in Caerwen.
By September, the evenings are drawing in and the air is sharp.
The ferry's timetable changes at the start of October.
The inn closes its upstairs rooms,
and the boats that have been out on the lake all summer are pulled up onto the shingle and turned over for the winter.
Autumn is the season of storms on Harrowmere.
Wind funnels down the valley from the north,
and the waves on the open water can reach a metre or more.
When a storm is forecast, the ferry stays in harbour, and the village waits.
Then, some time in December, the first hard frost arrives.
Ice forms along the edges of the lake,
thin at first, then thicker each night.
In a cold year it reaches all the way across to Sgeirra.
And the valley grows quiet once more, as it has every winter for as long as anyone can remember.
